title: THE HUMAN SCREAM
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the human scream: its volume and frequency range, why animals and babies scream, how screams bypass higher brain processing via the amygdala and trigger fight-or-flight before conscious recognition, the 2015 NYU study on the "roughness domain" shared only with alarms, the six or so scream types tied to emotions, screaming in pain and joy, scream queens and famous movie screams, a University of Utah MRI study of deathcore singer Will Ramos, screaming for pain control in hospitalized children, scream-based anxiety research, and primal scream therapy. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from Leslie.
topics: Invasion of the Body Snatchers scream

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on screaming, which Julia helped research, and say it was picked for its interesting range of reasons people scream.

segments.title: Scream basics: volume, frequency, and pitch
segments.summary: Screams reach roughly 80 to 120 decibels and 2,000 to 3,000 hertz, compared with normal speech. Chuck explains hertz as frequency and pitch as perception, and Josh notes a tone can have two different frequencies.

segments.title: Animal screams and why screaming works
segments.summary: Birds, seals, marmots, mountain lions and giraffes scream, and goat screaming videos are mentioned. Screams signal fear, distract predators and carry over long distances.

segments.title: Guinness record scream and neck strain
segments.summary: Chuck cites a Guinness record scream of 129 decibels, about one decibel under a jet engine. Screaming can strain the vocal area.

segments.title: Infant crying and cri du chat syndrome
segments.summary: A newborn's first scream clears mucus and signals life. A missing scream is alarming. Parents respond to their own baby's cries more quickly. Cri du chat syndrome, which has a cat-like cry, can be diagnosed initially from the cry.

segments.title: Fight or flight and the fawn response
segments.summary: Screams activate fight-or-flight. Chuck and Josh briefly discuss the fawn response and decline to re-explain fight or flight in detail.

segments.title: Scream pathway in the brain
segments.summary: Normal speech runs through higher brain processing, while screams are sent from the limbic system and amygdala directly to the brain stem and vocal anatomy, a faster express path.

segments.title: How the brain hears screams before conscious awareness
segments.summary: Hearing a scream goes through the ear and thalamus, and the sound is routed to the amygdala, triggering fight-or-flight before the higher brain finishes processing. Hosts describe this as an evolved scream-only pathway.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: The roughness domain and the 2015 NYU study
segments.summary: Screams sit in the roughness domain, amplitude modulation between about 30 and 150 hertz, which in human sounds is reserved for screams and shared with artificial alarms. A 2015 NYU study analyzed recorded sounds, had volunteers scream, rated scariness, and scanned amygdala activity, finding alarm and scream sounds triggered the most amygdala response. Screams also penetrate sleep more than neutral vocalizations.

segments.title: Types of screams: anger, pain, joy, sadness
segments.summary: The study identified about six non-speech scream types tied to emotions. Hosts discuss anger, fear, pain, extreme joy and pleasure, and sadness, and note that non-alarm joyful screams appear uniquely human, while some non-human primates scream in grief. Examples include Europe songs, Platoon and The Simpsons, and Toni Collette in Hereditary.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with transition back to screaming.

segments.title: Movie screams and scream queens
segments.summary: Hosts discuss scream queens, starting with Fay Wray in King Kong (1933) whose screams were made in post-production. They discuss Mike Shank's scream in the documentary about Wisconsin low-budget horror filmmaking, and men's screams in horror films, including Ben Burtt's scream in Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1978), Thomas Jane in The Mist and Bruce Campbell.
topics: Invasion of the Body Snatchers scream

segments.title: Horror actors and scream-related movie picks
segments.summary: Hosts mention Justin Long's new horror comedy Coyotes, Janet Leigh in Psycho, Neve Campbell in Scream, Mia Goth in the Maxxxine trilogy, and Nate Bargatze's movie crush pick of Scream.

segments.title: Death metal screaming and vocal MRI study
segments.summary: University of Utah researchers used dynamic MRI on deathcore singer Will Ramos of Lorna Shore. Normal singing showed little movement in the neck, while screaming showed much more activity, and the study explored how he avoids damaging his vocal cords.

segments.title: Screaming for pain control
segments.summary: A 2020 survey of hospitalized children found they felt liberation and calm after screaming, which helped manage pain. Parents and staff often try to stop them. Endorphins released in fight-or-flight may explain the pain relief. Screams are also being used to induce anxiety in research instead of electric shocks.

segments.title: Primal scream therapy
segments.summary: Primal scream therapy, founded by Arthur Janov and popular in the 1960s and 1970s, holds that childhood trauma is stored as primal pain released through screaming. Evidence is limited, and it may increase anxiety.
